summary: This proposed standard describes an end-to-end session identifier for IP-based multimedia communication. Endpoints, intermediaries and management systems can use it to identify a session end to end, associate several endpoints with a multipoint conference, and track sessions as they are redirected.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone call is passed through many helpers, it helps for the call to have one number all of them can see. This defines that single call number.

what is a nil uuid in sip

subtitle: A Session-ID header that gives a SIP call one identifier made of two UUIDs, one from each end.

tldr.problem: Call identifiers in SIP and H.323 differ in syntax, and devices such as session border controllers often rewrite them, so a session is hard to track end to end.
tldr.mechanism: Each endpoint makes a UUID and the Session-ID header carries both, as a local-uuid and a remote parameter. The pair forms the session identifier, and intermediaries must pass it through unchanged apart from the cases the RFC lists.
tldr.outcome: It lets operators troubleshoot, correlate forked calls, and link conference participants, and it obsoletes the pre-standard RFC 7329 with rules for talking to old implementations.

today: RFC 7989 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 7329, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The End-to-End Session Identifier
sections.content:
SIP and H.323 each have a globally unique call identifier, but they are unsuitable for tracking a session end to end. Their syntax differs, so the value cannot be exchanged when both protocols are used in one call. Devices such as session border controllers (RFC 7092) also change signaling, including the call identifier, as it passes through.

This document defines a new session identifier. The RFC states that it has been adopted by the ITU (H.460.27) for H.323 systems, and this document defines its use in SIP. It follows the requirements of RFC 7206 and specifies a backwards-compatibility approach for the pre-standard RFC 7329.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal call numbers get changed along the way, like a parcel being relabeled at each depot. A session identifier is a code that stays with the call all the way.

sections.title: Building the Identifier from Two UUIDs
sections.content:
The session identifier is a set of two UUIDs (RFC 4122), one per endpoint. The caller creates a new, previously unused UUID and the callee creates its own. The pair is written {A,B}, and {A,B} equals {B,A}. When only one is known, the other is the nil UUID, written {A,N}.

To avoid leaking user or device information, endpoints MUST generate version 4 (random) or version 5 (SHA-1) UUIDs, not MAC-based ones. A version 5 UUID uses a fixed namespace ID, and the name is the Call-ID value joined with the tag parameter of the From or To line. Stateless intermediaries that insert a Session-ID on an endpoint's behalf MUST use version 5. Once generated, an endpoint's UUID never changes for the session.

Two UUIDs matter because endpoints can be replaced. If Alice and Bob both call Carol, the sessions are {A,C} and {B,C}. If Carol's PBX joins the two legs, the merged call is {A,B}. Forking gives {A,B1}, {A,B2} and so on, and in a conference the focus uses the same UUID M for everyone: {A,M}, {B,M}, {C,M}.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side of the call makes up its own secret-looking code. The call's name is both codes together, so if one person is swapped out, you can still see which call it grew from.

sections.title: The Session-ID Header Field
sections.content:
The Session-ID header is single-instance and appears in all SIP messages an endpoint sends. Its value is a local-uuid (the sender's own UUID) followed by a remote parameter holding the peer's UUID. Each UUID is 32 characters of lowercase hexadecimal, and the nil UUID is 32 zeros. There MUST NOT be more than one remote parameter. It MUST be present except for backwards compatibility with RFC 7329.

An initial request carries the nil UUID as the remote value, because the initiator does not yet know the peer's. The final destination replaces it when it responds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message says "here is my code, and here is the code of the one I am talking to." If you do not know their code yet, you write a row of zeros.

sections.title: Endpoint and Intermediary Behavior
sections.content:
An endpoint MUST put its own UUID in local-uuid and the peer's UUID, if known, in remote. It MUST NOT change its own UUID for the session, including on retries after 4xx responses or timeouts, 3xx redirects, transfers via REFER, or an INVITE with Replaces. It records any non-nil local-uuid it receives as the peer's UUID. A message lacking Session-ID must not change what it believes about the peer. A CANCEL MUST carry the same Session-ID as the request it cancels.

An intermediary that complies MUST forward the same UUID values it received, with exceptions. When aggregating several forked responses, it MUST set local-uuid to the nil UUID. If an endpoint sent no UUID, an intermediary MAY assign one on its behalf, and it then becomes dialog-stateful. When it originates a message it SHOULD hold state for both UUIDs, and a stateless one MUST NOT insert a Session-ID. When it joins call legs it MUST build the header with the correct endpoint UUIDs, and when interworking SIP with H.323 it SHOULD pass the identifier between the legs.

A response whose non-nil local-uuid is not 32 octets long comes from a misbehaving implementation, so its Session-ID header MUST be discarded, though the response itself should still be checked under normal SIP rules.
sections.plainLanguage: You keep your own code for the whole call, no matter what. Helpers in the middle must pass codes along honestly and only make one up if the caller forgot to.

sections.title: Handling Remote UUID Changes
sections.content:
A peer's UUID can change because of service interactions, so endpoints and intermediaries MUST accept a peer's new UUID in defined conditions. When a mid-dialog request carries a new UUID, all responses to it MUST carry the new value as the remote parameter, unless a later successful transaction has a different one. If the receiver sends a 2xx or 3xx response, it MUST accept the new UUID. If it sends a failure response (4xx, 5xx or 6xx), it MUST NOT accept it, and later messages keep the previously stored value. An ACK for a 2xx or 3xx response with a new UUID is accepted; an ACK for a failure response is not.

A new UUID received in a response MUST be accepted. A new UUID in a CANCEL request MUST NOT be accepted, because CANCEL is not passed end to end and always carries the UUID from the original INVITE. An intermediary that accepts a new UUID SHOULD try to inform other endpoints, for example with a re-INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tells you they have a new code, you only write it down once the call has really moved on. If the call was refused, you keep the old code.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 7329
sections.content:
The earlier Session-ID in RFC 7329 carried a single UUID. The RFC says it was never standardized but has been heavily implemented and adopted by other standards bodies. Neither version carries version information, so the presence and order of a remote-uuid tells them apart.

A request with a remote-uuid comes from a standard implementation, and one without comes from a pre-standard one. A response with a non-nil 32-octet local-uuid differing from the endpoint's own UUID comes from a standard implementation. A response that repeats the same UUIDs in the same order, or contains only the original local-uuid, comes from a pre-standard one and MUST NOT be discarded. For the rest of such a dialog the sender keeps the order of the UUIDs, or sends only the single UUID received in the first response. A new dialog from a standard implementation still starts with a local-uuid and nil remote-uuid. Pre-standard implementations may be inconsistent within a dialog, and this MUST be tolerated.
sections.plainLanguage: There was an older, one-code version already in use. The new version spots which kind it is talking to by looking at whether a second code is there.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The identifier MUST NOT convey user or device information. A UA always creates a new UUID for each new session, so two unrelated sessions from the same UA cannot be linked through it. However, the identifier can reveal relationships between endpoints. In the RFC's example, an observer who sees the session identifier across Alice-Bob and Bob-Carol signaling can learn that Alice is in fact talking to Carol, even if the PBX changes everything else. It would not reveal who they are.

Extra parameters (generic-param) MUST NOT include user or device information, MUST NOT persist beyond the session and MUST NOT be reused across unrelated sessions. A privacy service following Section 5.3 of RFC 3323 MAY treat the header as nonessential, which impairs troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is random, so it does not say who you are. But if someone sees the same code on two calls, they can tell those calls belong together.
